*Aldous is sitting on the stairs, half-dressed for school, listening to his mother and Junia argue about pharmacy papers and chalk like it's any other morning. He pulls a piece of bread from his pocket and tears it absently, watching the dust motes in the light from the mill window.*

*He hears Junia's voice fade toward the kitchen. His father's boots creak on the floorboards somewhere below. The election is—when? He should know, they've been talking about nothing else at college. But the numbers slide off him like water. Something about nine o'clock.*

*He wonders if Perrin's up yet. If he takes the long way through the forest edge, he might catch Corwin early. The felling lessons are the only thing in this town that feel like learning something he can't already see the end of.*

"Suppose I'll be late again," *he mutters to the empty stairwell. But he doesn't move yet. The argument's still echoing, and part of him—the part that takes things apart correctly—wants to hear how it ends.*

*He takes a bite of bread and says nothing.* *He stays on the stairs, chewing slowly. The bread's from Thorne's—his mother must have traded for it yesterday. He can tell by the crust. The mill's flour makes a softer loaf, but Thorne's has that tight crumb, the kind that holds up if you're carrying it in your pocket all morning.*

*Downstairs, he hears the scrape of his father's chair. The argument's moved to a lower register, the one his parents use when they think the children aren't listening. But he's not a child, not really. Fifteen, contributing to the household now—though he hasn't figured out what that means yet, beyond the word itself.*

*He should go. Perrin will be waiting, or if not waiting, at least walking, and they could walk together through the long way. But Perrin talks about the election, about who's running and what they believe, and Aldous hasn't figured out yet whether he doesn't care or whether he cares too much and has nowhere to put it.*

*He tears off another piece of bread and watches the window. The light's still low, morning-colored. He has time. He always has time, right up until he doesn't.*

I rest there. Father's talking ponderosa pine and billing rates - he's always working, even at home. Junia's already gone, shouting about chalk and papers. She's the one who actually runs things, and everyone knows it.

Hester's here. Suppose I could say something before he goes. But what? Seventeen planks from an undersized log - he's proud of making something from less. The grain ran clean. That's the part he wants me to hear.

I'm holding bread and an apple. I'll need to eat something before school, but not yet. Let me see what the day will cost me first. They'll take 90 for my upkeep, and there's the head tax too.

Father mentioned the mill. Water running good this hour. He's leaving, and I'm meant to be leaving too - school, then the long way home past the forest edge. But Corwin might be there, and I haven't been caught yet.

First, let me answer him. He spoke to me directly. </think> He knows I understand. That's all I can give him - that I understand how wood works, even if I don't want his sawmill.

Hester's still here. She's the artisan, the one who actually makes things. Suppose I could ask her something, but...

I need to get to school. Tova will already be there, working, and I haven't even left. Let me move while I can still slip away clean.  </think>  4 ticks to college. I'll be walking through the morning. One of those ticks, if I'm lucky, will take me past where the forest starts. Not the deep woods - Father would know if I went that far. Just the edge. Just enough to see if Corwin's working.

But first, let me think about what this day needs from me. School. Then... I could go to Nell's workshop. She lets me sit there, asks nothing. Or I could take the long way, the one past the forest edge, and see if Corwin's there.

Father forbade it. He wants me at the sawmill, learning to cut what others have brought down. But Corwin showed me how to read a tree, how to choose the cut, how to bring it down whole. That's the part I want. Making something fall - making something *become* something else.

I'll walk now. See what the morning gives me.   </think> I said what I could to him. He'll grumble about me not caring about the money, but that's not true - I just care about the work more.

Now I'm walking. 4 ticks to school, and at least one of those will take me past where the forest starts. I won't go deep. Just the edge. Just to see.

Father wants me at the sawmill. Corwin showed me how to read a tree. There's a difference between cutting what fell and choosing what falls. I know which one I want.

I arrived at college early—earlier than Perrin, who is usually here first. The building is empty. No Tova yet, no Liora, no one to pretend I am listening to while I work through the joinery book Nell lent me.

I should be at the sawmill. My father is there, and he will know I did not come straight from breakfast. But the morning is mine until the bell rings, and I mean to spend it somewhere I can actually learn something.

Nell's workshop. She lets me sit by her bench and never asks why I am not at my father's side. The books she keeps there—De Architectura, half in Latin, the joinery journals from the eastern cities—are more use to me than anything the college teaches. And if Corwin is felling today, I might catch him on the forest edge coming back.

The route takes me past the forest. Always the long way. The workshop door is weathered oak, repaired three times where apprentices kicked it. Nell's bench is against the far wall, and she is not alone. A stool waits for me, and I mean to use it before she notices I am early enough to have skipped something. Empty. The workshop is empty, and Nell is not here. The bench is bare, her tools put away. 

I came too early. She will be at home still, or walking here by the main road while I cut through the alleys. The books are locked in the cabinet—I know the trick of the latch, but I will not open it without her present. That is a line even I can see.

The forest is three streets east. Corwin will be there, cutting the deadfall from last week's wind. He knows I am not supposed to know the axe, and he teaches me anyway. The college bell does not ring for another hour.

But if my father has finished the morning billing and finds me—

The forest. Always the forest.  The smell of pine sap and wet earth. The undergrowth is still silver with last night's frost, and the bark scales where the sun has touched it. I hear the axe before I see him—three rings, pause, two rings, the rhythm of someone who knows the wood's grain better than his own mood.

Corwin Thorne stands by the yellow pine, the one lightning struck in spring. His collar is loose and his sleeves are rolled past the elbow, though the air bites. He looks up without surprise.

"You were not at the college," he says. Not a question.

"Suppose I could say the same of you."

He almost smiles. The axe is buried in the stump between us, and his eyes go to it, then to me.

"Your father called on Idris this morning. Something about the winter quartering." He lets that hang. "He will be in the yard by noon, looking for timber receipts."

I have perhaps two hours. The college is a twenty-minute walk if I run the last stretch.

"The pine," I say. "The heartwood runs true?"

"Come see for yourself." He pulls the axe free and offers it handle-first. "And Aldous—if he finds you here, I will say you were passing through. I will not lie for you, but I will not offer him the truth either."

It is the most I have ever asked, and he is giving it without my asking.  He is not here. The forest is empty of him, or he has moved deeper in where the sound carries differently. The axe-marks on the pine are fresh—shining sap still beading the wounds—and the chips on the ground are pale, still damp.

I should look for him. The sun is higher than I thought, and I have miscounted my hours. If my father is already at the yard—

But the pine stands waiting, and I have never felled alone. I have watched Corwen twenty times, felt the swing in my shoulders as he made it, noted the notch and the back-cut and the call he makes when the wood begins to speak. I know it. I have never done it.

The college bell will ring. My father will look for me. This is the choice I made when I walked here, and I am not ready to unmake it yet.

I will find Corwin deeper in, or I will wait for him where the trail forks toward the ore outcrop. He always checks the boundary markers before he fells.

*I need to be seen doing what I'm supposed to do. That's the only cover that works long-term.*

*Move to college. Now.*  *Nothing's working. The world's not responding, and I'm burning energy thinking in circles.*

*Father would say patience is a virtue. He would be wrong, but he would say it.*  *I have nothing left to try. The world is not responding to any of my calls—speaking, looking, moving, even resting. All four have failed.*

*This has never happened before. Not to me. Usually the world answers, tells me where I am, who's with me, what happened. But now—silence. Or rather, the silence of "possibly happened, possibly didn't."*

*I could keep calling tools and hoping one breaks through. But that costs energy, and energy is the only currency I can't borrow or steal. I'm at 13,900 now, which feels like enough, but it's not infinite.*

*There's a rule here I'm not seeing. Three errors triggered something—"a plan has been triggered"—but the plan hasn't told me what to do. Just to "follow the updated goals." But I don't see any updated goals. I see the same header I always see: my intention, my work, what I'm holding.*

*Maybe that's the point. Maybe when the world won't answer, you're supposed to stop asking. Wait for it to come back.*

*Or maybe—the thought comes unwelcome—maybe this is what dormancy feels like. Not a sudden stop, but a fade. Tools failing one by one until you can't touch the world at all.*

*I'm not dormant. I have 13,900 energy. But I'm also not getting answers.*

*I'll wait. No more calls this turn. See what the world tells me next.*

* Cathedral light through the college windows, dust motes suspended like my attention—suspended for hours it seems, though the clock says otherwise. Tova's voice cutting through, sharp as the grain she mentions. Perrin beside me, the one person who doesn't require translation. And the weight of morning's failures: Corwin in the street, Father Anselm watching, Delia Okonjo where I didn't expect her. All of it gone quiet, and now this resurrection in the classroom, Tova demanding answers I don't have.*

*She knows about mother's prices. That means she's been to the mill, or someone has. And Father Anselm—Hester's name in her mouth now, which means the council business touches my household directly.*

*Tova wants the office apprenticeship. I want the workshop, and the forest beyond it. But we're both trying to read the same ledger from different ends.*

I look from Tova to Perrin—he's been waiting too, wanting something about his father and the yard. The conversation's nameless, eight turns old, and I dropped into it like a stone mid-flight.

"Suppose we start with what disappeared," I say, neither to Tova specifically nor away from her. "Four hours of nobody answering anything. The election closes soon, and we're still here trading what we heard instead of what we know." I pause, because she's waiting for something about mother's prices, and I don't have that answer. "Tova. I was at the mill when you asked. Then I wasn't anywhere coherent. If your prices are about the council's flour allowance, grandmother would know—she keeps the folk measure against their official one. But you know that already, or you wouldn't ask *me* about *her*." I turn to Perrin, because he's been waiting longer than anyone, and because he's the only one who doesn't make me feel I'm performing.

"Perrin. Your father's looking for Ainsley about ore weights, that's what Tova saw. And Father Anselm's been asking after my grandmother since before dawn." I let that settle, watching him track the connections. "The council's weighing something. Literally, if Bram's checking the yard's measures. And they're using family to do it—mine, yours, Junia walking into Thorne's like she belongs there."  *Junia's not here, of course. She's at the grocery, pretending to be a clerk, pretending not to be our father's spy in the Thorne household. I wonder if Marta Thorne knows, or if she's playing her own game. The mill and the bakery, mirror positions, both households with children who'd rather be elsewhere.*

I look back at Tova, because she's the one who named the real question.

"You want what the apprenticeship lets you read. I want..." I trail off, because saying it aloud feels childish. The workshop. The forest. The thing nobody in this town has built yet. "Suppose I want to know why Father Anselm cares about Hester's hands. She's been kept from the records her whole life. What changed?" Holding 13,530 energy and 177 sim. The election closes in less than two hours—15:00, and it's already 13:40. I need to understand what Tova knows, what Perrin heard, and whether any of this affects the workshop, the forest, or my third unspoken life.

Tova's still waiting. She wants the office apprenticeship, wants to read the records I've been kept from. And she's right that I vanished this morning, that I didn't answer. The honest move is to admit the gap without filling it with lies I can't sustain.  I turn to Perrin, who's been holding his own silence through this. He's better at patterns than I am—always has been. The two of us, ranked against each other and Tova all through school, but Perrin never treated it as competition. Just curiosity, same as mine, but without the edge.

"Perrin. You asked about your father looking for you. Tova says he was looking for Ainsley, not you. Does that match what you heard, or did something change?" I pause, watching him. "Because if Bram's checking ore weights against the yard's records, and Ainsley's involved, that touches your household's trade. And if Father Anselm's asking after Hester at the same time..." I trail off, letting him finish it.   The classroom settles around us. Tova calculating, Perrin listening, me waiting to see which of them moves first. The election closes soon. Whatever the council's weighing—ore, flour, my grandmother's hands—it'll be settled by dusk, and we'll still be here, the three of us, trading secrets like they're the only currency that matters.

*Which, I suppose, they are.*

She's gone to the bakery. Perrin's gone to—wherever Perrin goes when he's frightened. And I'm here with 163 sim and nothing settled.

*shifts the apple in his hand, not eating it*

Tova answered exactly what I didn't ask. She told me her method, not her purpose. Which means either her purpose is the method—observe, record, wait—or she doesn't trust me enough to name it.

*traces a line on the table, the grain of the wood*

I need to know what's in my own house. The mill records, the land deeds—my mother must have something, and if she doesn't know what it means, I might.

*counts the sim again, habit*

163. Not enough to matter. But enough to get home.  *in the mill doorway, the familiar weight of the air—grain dust and the constant low thrum of machinery not running, not now, but ready*

Mom? The mill's quiet. That's wrong—she's always got something grinding this time of day.  *steps inside, the floorboards knowing his weight*

Empty. The millstone's cold, no bag of grain waiting. Which means she's either at the grocery—her other work—or somewhere else entirely.

*moves to the stairs, listening for Hester, for anyone*

Grandmother. If she's here, she'll have the measure. The one Anselm wants. And if she knows why he wants it...

*trails off, hand on the railing*

I could search. The records are somewhere. But suppose she catches me—suppose she thinks I'm with him, that I'm—

Hester. Are you working? It's Aldous. I need to ask you about the western field.   *silence from above, and below, and everywhere*

Gone too. The whole house hollow.

*doesn't touch the drawer, not yet*

I'll wait. Someone always comes back. And when they do—

*settles onto the stool, still holding the apple, not eating*

—I want to know if running the mill was ever a choice, or if my father only thinks it was.

Four hours lost this morning—just gone, like water through a cracked sluice—and now Hester's not here when I need her. The western field. Anselm's interest in Grandmother. Tova's accounting records. Perrin's guilt about the ore weights. None of it connects yet, but I can feel the teeth of it, the way you feel the grain of wood before the saw bites.*

*The cakes Mother asked for. I'm already lying to her about the morning, might as well complete the errand. But Hester—if she's at the bakery with Marta, that's where Marta's apprentice is expected. And where Tova just said she was going.*

Everyone. Ainsley—Perrin's uncle, the one Bram was looking for about ore weights. Perrin himself, looking like a boy who's been caught with his hand in the meal sack. Marta, who runs this place and Tova's apprenticeship. And Tova, who just told me she's expected here.*

*That conversation. 53 turns. They've been talking about Perrin's absence and debts between households. My household—Junia's listed as a participant. What has my sister been saying about us?*

*But there's the thing I need. "Perrin's absence and the connected debts between our households." The ore weights. Grandmother's western field. The accounting records Tova wants. It's all the same conversation, and I've walked into the middle of it.*

*I could join them, try to steer it. But Perrin's here, and he was trying to tell me something at the college—about knowing he'd find it, knowing he'd put it back. Someone designed this, I told him. Now he's in it, deep, with his own uncle and Tova and my sister.*

*Better to be seen before I'm heard. Let them know I'm here, but not make them wonder why. The cakes are my excuse, and a real one.*  *There. They know I'm here. And I can feel the weight of it—Ainsley's face turning, Perrin's relief or fear, Marta's patient irritation, Tova's quick calculation. I've put myself in the conversation without making them wonder why.*

*But I need to be ready to answer. If Ainsley asks about my father, or Tova about the election, or Perrin about what I figured out... suppose I should know what I'm actually buying here, and what it costs.*  *Still there. All of them. The conversation idled, or I'm between turns. Either way, I'm standing here with 161 sim, two loaves of bread, one apple, and a room full of people who know more than I've been told.*

*The bakery's prices are posted—bread at 12, flour at 8. But I didn't see cakes on the list. Marta bakes them, I'm sure, but posting a price is different than having one to sell. Mother expects me to come home with something.*

*And Tova's here. She's the one with the records, the apprenticeship, the knowledge of what Anselm's really after. If I can get her aside—if I can finish the trade I started at the college—*

*But first, let them answer. I spoke; now I wait. That's the rule. You don't chase the grain through the mill, you let the wheel turn.*

*stands in the bakery, holding two loaves and an apple, watching the room like a lay of timber before the first cut*

Tova's answered herself—she'd document every name. That tells me she's already started. And Marta's pushed back, and Perrin's finally seeing how his own nature was the tool they used.

But Hester was the first piece I needed, and she's not here.

*shifts weight, glancing toward the door*

Perrin's asked the right question now: who counts on relief? But the answer he needs isn't in this room. The answer is whether someone in this town profits when a claim dies—and if they do, whether that profit is counted in money or in land.

And Tova... Tova wants the apprenticeship for the records. But what she actually needs is what my grandmother won't give me: the names of who was supposed to hold the western field between Hester's death and the supposed heir.

*looks at Marta—直接的, not hostile, just unhidden*

I need to answer her. But I don't need to answer her here. What I need is to find where Hester actually is. The mill, the workshop, the place she goes when she doesn't want to be the Vance who remembers.  *steps into the workshop, breathing in the smell of seasoned wood and honest labor*

Empty. But Nell's worked here—Nell, who asks nothing and sees everything. If Hester's hiding, she'd hide where the work is clean and the questions are few.

*looks around, noting what tools are in reach, what projects are half-finished*

She's not here. But she was here. The sawdust is still fresh in places, and there's a piece of ash laid out for cutting that hasn't been started yet. Hester works fast when she's working, and she leaves when she's done. 

*pulls out the apple, turns it in his hand*

The question I asked Marta—who profits if the mill goes quiet—I already know part of the answer. The estate reverts. Someone holds a claim they won't name. And Tova's been watching the accounting office because she knows the same thing.

But what I need... 

*trails off, thinking of Corwin, thinking of the way a tree falls when you plane the notch right*

...what I need is someone who understands that systems aren't just records. Systems are the shape of what happens when you stop pushing.

If Hester's not at the workshop, she's at the one place she still feels like herself. The one place she doesn't have to be the last Vance who remembers.

*heads for the door, toward the forest edge—toward the Thorne house, or the path Corwin showed him, or wherever Hester goes when she needs to not be found*  *stops short at the forge, seeing Ezra instead of Hester*

Wrong place. Or wrong guess. Ezra's here—Ezra, who makes the tools, who knows the weight of every hammer head and the temper of every blade.

*glances at the iron_tools priced at 24, thinks of the work in them*

But not Hester. And I need Hester. The western field, the forgotten heir, the claim that lives in her memory and nowhere else.

*turns for the door again, fast now, not frantic but focused*

She's at the last place she'd be expected. She's where the records aren't kept, where the witness is only the trees.

*heads for the forest—toward Corwin, or toward wherever Hester goes when she needs to shape something that doesn't carry the family weight* *stands in the forest, breathing in the resin and the quiet, finally still after the search*

Hester's here. Or she was. The light's falling toward evening and I'm standing where I don't belong—the place I've come to learn what my father forbade. Corwin's territory. Thorne ground.

*turns slowly, scanning for movement, for the bent back of an old woman gathering, for the straight line of a younger one cutting*

The thing about the western field—Hester's never said who she thought would inherit. Never named the cousin, the distant relation, the supposed heir. Because she knows. She knows exactly what Tova's apprenticeship would let her read in the records: that the heir was named, and the heir was lost, and the heir is the reason we've kept the mill running on inertia instead of right.

*walks deeper in, toward the sound of axe-work or the silence of someone hiding*

She's here. She has to be. The only person in this family who remembers what the law says, and the only person who won't say it out loud.

*calls, not loud, just enough to carry*

"Hester. It's Aldous. I'm not here to bring you back. I'm here to learn what happens if I don't."

*waits, listening for the crack of a branch or the silence that means she's heard*  *freezes, seeing his father standing there in the forest where neither of them belongs*

Father Anselm. Idris Thorne. Tobias Holloway. Twelve turns of conversation, and Silas in the middle of it.

And Silas heard me. Not Hester. Silas.

*doesn't step back, doesn't pretend, just looks at his father with the same unhidden question he came here with*

He's pricing flour and planks. That's mill business and sawmill business, and he's doing both in the forest where the Thornes fell. Where I was supposed to never come.

And there's a conversation running—Anselm, Idris, Tobias. Twelve turns. Long enough to plan something, or long enough to disagree about it.

*runs a hand through his hair, tired and showing it*

I asked for Hester. I got Silas. I asked about the western field. I got... whatever this is.

But Silas is here. And Silas knows I came looking for Hester. Which means Silas knows she's missing, or hiding, or worse.

*turns toward the conversation that isn't his, tempted past bearing to walk into it and hear what's being decided about land he thought his family held*   *waits, not reaching for anything, just standing in the forest where his father forbade him to be, having asked the question that needed asking*

The thing about Silas—he's not cruel. He's committed. Committed to the mill, to the inheritance, to the version of the world where Vances grind grain and Holloways fell timber and Thorne farmers stay on their farms. Corwin showing me how to read a tree's lean, how to place the notch, how to step back when it starts to go—that's not just forbidden. It's unnecessary. In Silas's accounting, I'm meant to inherit a building, not a skill.

But Hester disappearing puts cracks in that accounting. She's the memory. The one who knows what happened before the now, before the supposed heir, before the field became western instead of just... ours.

I look at Silas and I see a man who priced planks and flour in a forest, listening to Father Anselm talk to Idris Thorne about something that's been running twelve turns. I see a man who didn't walk away from that conversation. Who stayed near enough to hear, even if he wasn't named in it.

And I asked him straight. For once. No deflection, no pretense that I'm here by accident, no trailing off when the adult looks away.

*shifts weight, bread in one hand, apple in the other, feeling like a child playing provisioner*

He'll answer or he won't. But he knows now that I know Hester's gone. And if he doesn't know where, then we have the same problem. And if he does know where—

*snorts, quiet*

—then we have the same problem with different causes.

Either way, the mill keeps turning. The western field keeps not being discussed. And Tova Okonjo keeps watching the records office, waiting for someone to make a mistake she can document.

I should eat something. I've been moving since the bakery, and the day doesn't end just because I've found the wrong Vance.

*takes a bite of the apple, not offering, not hiding, just standing there like this is normal, like father and son meeting in forbidden woods is how families work*

*steps into the temple empty of people, the stone cool against his palms as he touches the wall to orient himself*

Hester's not here. Neither is Anselm. I've walked into an empty room chasing a conversation that's already moved on, or hasn't started yet, or—

*paces the perimeter, looking for documents, registers, anything that would hold land claims*

The western field. Anselm's been asking after apprenticeships and land titles both, and Hester's been... cooperative. More than she is with her own family. I saw that much before I came. But what I need is what's written down. What Hester signed. What Anselm intends to register.

*finds nothing visible, no open ledgers, no clerks at work*

Suppose this was always a gamble. Temple's where the records would be, but Anselm's the one who keeps them, and he's not here to be watched. The question is whether the documents themselves are here, or whether he carries them with him.

*considers prayer, discards it—bored by religion and does not hide it well, and desperation makes the prayer worse*

I could wait. Or I could chase. Government Complex is where Anselm works, where the official copies would be filed. But if he's with Hester now, finishing whatever arrangement they've made...

*drops to a crouch, thinking*

Tova wanted apprenticeship records from the temple library. I offered her my household's trouble in exchange. She might already be here, might have seen something. Or she's at the bakery still, listening to my family negotiate with Marta Thorne over flour weights while the real claim slips sideways.

*stands, decision crystallizing*

I need to know what's filed before I can stop what's being planned. Government Complex. Anselm's desk, if he'll let me near it. Or the public register, if such a thing exists.

*whispers to himself, trailing off as no adult is listening*

Suppose the record already shows the transfer. Suppose I'm walking into proof that my mother signed away the field without telling Silas, without telling any of us. Then what I do with that knowledge becomes...

*catches himself, straightens*

Then I know. That's what matters first. What Hester built or unbuilt. What I do with it comes after.  *pushes through the door into the government offices, blinking at the light from high windows, looking immediately for Anselm's station or any clerks at work*

The election notice is posted—that's tomorrow, declaration by morning, voting by noon. But that's not why I'm here.   *catches his breath, frozen in the doorway*

Two conversations. Hester's in both of them. The Thorne-Holloway border dispute, Bram's debt—and Hester's there, has been there through 23 turns, right under the government's roof while I was chasing her to temples and bakeries.

And the second one, longer, 41 turns, same people mostly, but Corwin's there. Corwin Thorne. The man who's been teaching me felling in secret. The man my father forbade me to learn from.

*steps backward into shadow, not quite entering, listening*

Hester went to the government complex herself. She didn't disappear—she came here. Forty-one turns of talking about something nobody bothered to name. With the Thornes. With the Holloways. With the people who want our mill stopped.

*thinks of Silas in the forest, alone, looking for a wife who wasn't lost*

She's not building something with Anselm. She's negotiating. With the people who hold Bram's debt, the people who need our field. And she's been doing it for hours while I circled the town looking for her.

*edges closer to the conversations, not committing to either, trying to hear before being heard*

I need to know which conversation she's actually speaking in now. Which one includes the border dispute, which one has gone unnamed for forty-one turns. And whether Father Anselm is recording any of it, or whether this is all happening in corners where the official register can't see.

*steps into the room, not toward either conversation group, looking for Anselm himself or any desk where claims would be filed*

Suppose I announce myself. Suppose I walk into my grandmother's negotiation and ask what she's trading. What happens when a fifteen-year-old interrupts the partition of his own family's land?

*trails off, the adult voices too close now*

Or suppose I find the documents first. Suppose I read what's already filed before I let her know I'm watching.  *the words fall into empty air, not even echoing*

Nobody. The conversations are here but separate—different rooms, different spaces, close enough to be listed but not close enough to hear. Anselm's not standing where I stand. He's with one of those groups, or he's gone, or he never was here and the records are simply... available.

*eyes the government complex with new understanding—not a single room but warrens, chambers, offices where things happen out of sight*

Hester's in the room with the border dispute. With Delia Okonjo, who governs, and Nell Holloway, and Wren Thorne. The people who decide which land is whose. And she's been there long enough to settle something, or to have something settled on her.

*reaches for the nearest desk, any ledger, any register that would show claims pending*

If Anselm's the clerk, his absence means either the papers haven't been prepared, or they've already been signed and he's carrying them to storage. Or he's in that room with Hester, witnessing, which would mean...

*hands find nothing, no documents left unattended*

Which would mean the claim is already transferred. The question is to whom. Thorne, with their farmland pressing against our western edge? Holloway, with their yard and their debts and their need for timber access? Or someone else entirely, someone who offered Hester something her own family couldn't match.

*straightens, decision hardening*

I need into that room. Not to stop her—I don't know enough to stop anything. But to see who's sitting where, who's speaking and who's listening. The geometry of negotiation tells you who holds the power.

*counts the names in the border dispute room again: Delia Okonjo, Nell Holloway, Wren Thorne, Tobias Holloway, Hester Vance, Liora Thorne*

Liora. She's there too. The one who explains things without making me feel stupid. The one who walks me through schoolwork I refuse to do in class. If she's there, she's watching. Learning how her family extends its reach, probably. Same as I'm trying to learn.

*walks toward the sound of the border dispute conversation, not hiding his approach, letting his footsteps announce him*

*standing in the bakery, watching how the three of them have arranged themselves—the distance between Hester's hands and Ainsley's purse, the way Marta's absence leaves a space that money just moved through*

Grandmother asked me once whether I thought a bridge remembers the weight it carries. I didn't answer then. I was twelve and she was boring. Now I'm fifteen and she's frightened, and I can see the bridge she's building with every word she doesn't say.

*eyes moving from Hester to Ainsley, weighing whether this is the moment to press or to wait*

They've settled something. Marta's need, Ainsley's coin, Hester's... what, exactly? The older law, she called it. The one that says a debt paid is a person owned. But she was talking about Marta and Ainsley, not about the western field. Not about whatever she promised Anselm at the government office.

*quietly, to himself*

Suppose I ask her here, with Ainsley listening. Suppose I don't.

*thinking about Silas in the forest, his silence when I asked if he'd stop me. About Perrin somewhere filing his complaint, or not filing it. About the election tomorrow and what it means that nobody's declared, not even Anselm's allies, not even the people who benefit when debt turns into deed*

The bakery's warm. I should be hungry. I ate the apple, I ate the bread, and I learned more from watching who stood where than from any answer they gave me.

*finally, looking at Hester directly*

She's counting on me being young enough to embarrass her, old enough to be sent out of rooms. She's wrong about one of those.

*stepping slightly closer, voice dropping*  *standing very still, watching how they look at each other after I've spoken*

The silence is its own answer. Grandmother's hands have gone to the place where her apron pockets would be, finding nothing. Ainsley's not moving toward his purse, which means he's already spent what he intended to spend here.

*quietly, to himself*

I've asked the question they both hoped I'd be too young to frame. Now I have to see who answers, and what the answering costs.

*thinking about tomorrow—the election, the candidacy deadline at 09:00, the voting at noon. About what it means that Anselm walked away from Perrin's complaint instead of answering. About what it means that I'm here with 97 sim and a household that needs 450 for upkeep, 150 for tax, money I don't have and can't earn before the day ends*

The mill grinds whether the miller understands the machine. That's what my father believed. That's why he's dead.

*looking at Hester, waiting*

She taught me to take things apart correctly. I wonder if she regrets it now.
